He wouldn't say. Instead, Falvey called it "a matter of public and political controversy."

  • He finished law school in 2017 and has about six years of real legal practice outside his clerkships.
  • In 2020, he worked for Senate Republicans as they rushed ultra-conservative Amy Coney Barrett onto the Supreme Court.
  • After a federal court ruled South Carolina's congressional map racially discriminatory, Falvey helped defend it at the Supreme Court.
  • He represented Douglass Mackey, the influencer behind a scheme to trick Clinton voters into "voting" by text.
  • He has spent years inside Leonard Leo's network and the Federalist Society machine.

Here's what that tells you about Trump's criteria for these nominees: Qualifications? Independence? Proven loyalty?

If Falvey will duck a basic fact under oath to win Trump's approval, imagine what he'll do when a case Trump cares about lands on his docket.

We're not having it. Demand Justice PAC is fighting for courts that protect the people, and that means exposing every one of Trump's cronies before they get anywhere near a lifetime seat on the bench.

With Senate Democrats preparing to choose their next leader, the two contenders for the job took notably different approaches with their leadership PAC and joint fundraising committee money, .

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s leadership PAC distributed a net $252,500 to candidates and party committees during the cycle, according to an OpenSecrets analysis of Federal Election Commission filings. By comparison, Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland directed $262,000 to fellow candidates and party committees through his leadership political action committee and helped four battleground Senate candidates raise more than $421,000 through joint fundraising committees. 

The contrast offers a window into their different approaches to political giving ahead of the Dec. 1 vote for majority leader, after Democrats won control of the chamber. Van Hollen wrote more checks directly to candidates and supplemented them with joint fundraising committees, while Schumer’s leadership PAC gave a larger share of its money to party committees.

items.title: Your guide to having tough conversations this holiday season.
items.author: SRS0=C+a8=JO=mail135.sea51.mcsv.net=bounce-mc.us19_228507186.17295094-8782042e9f@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content:
We are a deeply polarized people. Social media makes it easy for us to surround ourselves with people who feel and act the same way. Our relationships with family and friends are unique in that we’re bonded socially for reasons often beyond our political and social values. This might mean you’re confronted with conversations you haven’t had the chance to practice before. Or, you may have watched people online host them without an attempt to stay in relationship – like a takedown video on TikTok that doesn’t leave room for repair.

As you engage with your community this holiday season, here are some tools to navigate tough conversations. Remember, all of these are only suggestions; relationships are unique and complex, and these best practices might not be best for you. I hope that they help you feel grounded and resourced to say the hard thing, share your point of view, and listen to others. Even if it feels futile, trying to bridge the divide between you and someone else is part of the work of forging togetherness on a larger scale. Here’s where to start.

Often, confrontation isn’t as effective as a nuanced conversation about a tricky topic. Consider leading a generative conversation by leading with your feelings, using “I” statements, and being vulnerable about your own journey with the topic(s) at hand. Please note: if calling someone out is a more direct and straightforward way to start the conversation and feels more generative to you, please do so.

Start from a place of empowerment.We all have the tools to dismantle oppression and reimagine spaces for all of us to thrive. You can start conversations with that mindset, which will enable your audience to see themselves as part of the solution, and not just the problem. You can say things like, “What can we do together?” “What tools do we have as a family?” “How can we show up best in our neighborhood?”

Don’t wait for something to react to.Most of the work regarding dismantling white supremacy happens as a reaction to a single incident. But for this work to be sustainable, we – especially those with privilege – need to get comfortable with the discomfort of this work proactively, not just as a reaction. Bring it up directly, perhaps by naming how a recent interaction made you feel.

There is no such thing as the “best” time.Many people are hesitant to get into tough conversations during the holidays, a time that can feel precious and “distanced” from the tension of everyday life. But there’s rarely a “best” time for difficult conversations. Consider instead: how can I host this conversation in the most generative way at this moment? How can I start this conversation now to create more space for it in the future?

Center whiteness, not Blackness (or other marginalized identities).When discussing racism specifically, many try to defend or validate marginalized communities. But as you do, don’t forget to name the harm of whiteness and colonization, not just those harms. When we focus the conversation on harmful actions, it leads more directly to changing these actions, not just building empathetic ties.

For example, this can look like naming the ongoing oppression led by the Israeli state when discussing Palestine. Or, naming the ongoing oppression the U.S. places on the Indigenous communities here.

Remember, no community needs to be validated by another to “deserve” respect. We all deserve respect. We need to adjust our actions and recognize our shortcomings to provide it, and reckon with the harm being caused.

You might want to start this conversation for a variety of reasons. Perhaps you want to see more accountability, or you simply want your family to know how their words and actions make you feel. Take a moment to honor what you’d like to see come out of this conversation, and you can even share that openly as the conversation progresses.

Hold your loved ones accountable. Ensure that you’re no longer tolerating their statements. Note how their continued racism will affect your relationship, and be prepared to stand firm. Remember that accountability is a practice of love, and so is setting boundaries for you and yours.

Demonstrate the actions you’ve taken to dismantle white supremacy in your own life. Use examples of what you’ve learned and unlearned in your own education. Be vulnerable about where you’re still growing – because we all have space to improve! And note how else you’re moving forward.

If you feel resourced, you can use this time to invite this person to join in – perhaps by reading a book together, having further discussions, etc. If that’s not available to you at the moment, you can offer to check in with them later to see how they’re progressing. Consider sharing a TikTok video you saw recently, or recommending a topical video for your family to watch.

Tough conversations with loved ones are not easy. If you have the opportunity, make a self-care plan for before, during, and after. Beforehand, practice some deep breathing and grounding exercises. Remember to check in with your breath and body during the conversation. And, plan for some time to decompress afterward, whether that’s scheduling time to decompress with a friend or therapist, taking a long walk later, journaling, etc. It might also be helpful to write some talking points and goals beforehand to help you feel more comfortable.

items.title: Trump’s new, dumb plan to stymie congressional subpoenas
items.author: delivery_20261125061502.48601725.7339@bounce.slate.com
items.content:
We’re releasing this week’s one day early so as not to interrupt your Thanksgiving holiday. We also have some important announcements about the newsletter at the bottom of the page. Thanks, as ever, for reading!

Last week, President Donald Trump pulled out his favorite Sharpie to do what he does best: sign an executive order awarding himself unprecedented power that will result in a nasty legal fight. This latest order has to do with executive privilege and attempts to shield all communications between the White House and federal agencies and contractors from the incoming Democratic congressional majorities who have pledged to investigate the Trump administration. It’s a transparent attempt to thwart congressional oversight into the administration’s numerous dealings, ranging from the White House ballroom project to violent immigration enforcement practices to the ongoing upheaval at Nvidia. The order is classic Trump, setting up the legal groundwork to push back against Congress’ authority in order to protect himself and his allies. However, like many of the executive orders signed during his second term, this latest one tees up a larger constitutional question about the extent of executive branch privilege versus congressional control. Ultimately, the outcome is unlikely to favor the president.

“In order to protect and serve the American people, the executive branch must be able to work closely with its employees and contractors on sensitive matters without fear that confidential information will be released to unauthorized third parties,” is how the president kicked off his executive order. It goes on to claim that Congress can’t seek information from executive branch departments, agencies, employees, or contractors “without a valid legislative purpose that does not intrude on core Executive functions.” The order ends by demanding that federal employees and contractors notify and coordinate with the White House if they receive requests for information related to congressional investigations. If they don’t comply, they can expect contracts to be terminated and could even face debarment—a blacklist that prevents them from ever getting a government contract again.

This executive order is a culmination of recent Trump administration attempts to mount a counterattack on the incoming Democratic-majority Congress. It started when a U.S. attorney in Texas sent out a slew of letters to members of Congress accusing them of engaging in unlawful activity after they pledged to investigate the administration. Then, last week, White House counsel Will Scharf issued a directive to all federal agencies stipulating that they get “approval” from the White House before agreeing to appear before any congressional committee. The last act came out Friday in the form of this new executive order. 

“This desperate Executive Order is totally unprecedented and blatantly unlawful. Federal contractors are paid with taxpayer dollars, not Trump’s personal billions (made illegally on the side),” the House Judiciary Committee account posted on X. “Public contractors have both a duty and a right to speak truthfully when Congress calls, and Congress has a duty to investigate and stamp out all the waste, fraud, kickbacks, shakedowns and corruption choking the government and driving up costs.”

While the White House is attempting to assert the doctrine of executive privilege over any and all communications between the executive branch and federal employees and contractors it hires, this isn’t historically how executive privilege has worked. It is a constitutionally protected right, defined as the president’s ability to withhold documents or information in their possession or in possession of the executive branch from the legislative or judicial branches of government. The Supreme Court has affirmed that it’s necessary in order to allow the president to carry out their duties and be free to discuss issues candidly without fear that the deliberations could be made public. Up until this point, as Joyce Vance, a former U.S. attorney for Alabama, recently noted, executive privilege has been understood to protect limited internal deliberations, “not commercial dealings between the government and contractors using public money.” 

The extent of executive privilege was famously put to the test during the Watergate scandal, when former Republican President Richard Nixon’s White House faced a criminal indictment. Nixon argued that his recorded conversations with his staff should be covered by executive privilege, thereby shielding him from a federal subpoena. The Supreme Court disagreed, concluding that neither the doctrine of separation of powers nor the executive branch’s need for confidentiality justified absolute presidential privilege, with limited exceptions for military or diplomatic affairs. The decision has remained untouched ever since, with executive privilege understood to not supersede “the fundamental demands of due process of law in the fair administration of justice.” 

While the White House is pressure testing executive privilege in the context of congressional investigations, it has also been using this strategy in the ongoing litigation over the future of the Kennedy Center. In that case, when lawyers for Ohio Rep. Joyce Beatty attempted to get the Trump administration to hand over dozens of emails and text messages between White House aides, the president’s legal team argued that its communications should be granted executive privilege in order to protect the White House’s ability to speak candidly and confidentially with staff. Judge Christopher R. Cooper, appointed by the Obama administration, is overseeing this case and has indicated an inclination to decide that some but not all of the president’s communications should be protected. It will come down to the context of the conversations: Were they about policy related to the Kennedy Center or about the “color of carpets”? 

The administration’s right to executive privilege will weigh against Congress’ right to oversight, and there is plenty of case law and federal law that support Congress’ authority to check the executive branch. Consider the 1967 case , when the Supreme Court affirmed that Congress’ oversight power “comprehends probes into departments of the Federal Government to expose corruption, inefficiency or waste,” concluding that “motives alone would not vitiate an investigation which had been instituted by a House of Congress if that assembly’s legislative purpose is being served.” 

There’s also the 1975 case Eastland v. United States Servicemen’s Fund, in which SCOTUS similarly concluded that “in determining the legitimacy of a congressional act we do not look to the motives alleged to have prompted it.” This all boils down to how the courts have long made clear that the relevant question isn’t why Congress is investigating a certain issue; “it’s solely whether the investigation has an objectively legitimate purpose,” Steve Vladeck, a law professor at Georgetown University, explained in his One First newsletter. 

Last time we checked, investigating potential acts of executive branch corruption, like if donors to Trump’s ballroom project received deferential treatment, and violations of federal law, which include if the Epstein files were publicly released according to the Epstein Files Transparency Act, squarely fall under a legitimate legislative purpose. 

It’s also worth mentioning that there are numerous federal laws that protect federal employees’ right to speak with Congress. The Lloyd–La Follette Act of 1912 guarantees federal employees the right to directly share information with Congress without interference or denial; Congress passed the act after the Roosevelt administration tried to ban federal employees from speaking with the legislative body unless they went through a federal agency department head. Without it, as Iowa Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley aptly explained back in 2018, “we would have an aristocratic government, one that would be dominated by the executive branch.”

Incoming chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee Maggie Hassan warned federal contractors that the president’s executive order “does not override their obligation to comply with congressional requests for information or subpoenas.”

We’ll have to wait and see how the fight over executive privilege plays out, at least until the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027, and Democrats can officially begin their investigations and issue subpoenas. They’ll have two years to accomplish their accountability agenda, and now, with Trump’s latest order, they may need to bake in time for lengthy legal fights.

“This new EO, dressed up in fancy talk about executive privilege and enhancing efficiencies, is nothing but a naked ploy to try and protect the perpetrators of this corruption,” Lisa Gilbert, co-president of the consumer advocacy group Public Citizen, said in a statement. “It will not succeed. Sunlight is coming, and corrupt administration insiders and contractors, both, will have to face the American people.”

It is not always easy to understand what Donald Trump intends to do, but it is always easy to tell when he is worried. Right now, he is terrified of congressional oversight, and he is keeping every option open to block it.

Trump's second term has been the most corrupt in American history. Barely a week goes by without news of another scheme to enrich him, his family or his advisers.

Corporate leaders have showered him and his causes with gifts. Foreign governments and their leaders have poured money into his family's crypto venture, provided a $400 million luxury jet for his use, and invested alongside his relatives.

Then there are the Epstein files. Congress passed bipartisan legislation requiring their release, only to see the Justice Department answer with heavy redactions and millions of withheld pages, in a file that mentions Trump thousands of times.

It is no wonder that Trump is worried. He has good reason to be.

His administration has been preparing for this moment for months.

items.title: Trump hasn't changed, and I can prove it
items.author: 1axbqu49uff75phphrh5snssvmfyhlp6soxb6b@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Every time the legacy media declares Donald Trump cured of election denialism, the symptoms flare up again. The latest relapse came over the weekend, when Trump was asked on Fox News about reports that the FBI had been hacked.

He found a “positive spin” on the hack. “Maybe we’ll learn things that we would have never learned otherwise,” he said. “… Maybe we’ll learn about the voter fraud, all the voter fraud that took place.”

Which election did he mean? He didn’t say. With Trump, it hardly matters.

In late October, Trump said he would respect the results “if they’re honest elections.” On election night, as Republican losses mounted, he told The New York Times he was “absolutely willing to accept those results.” The legacy media swooned.

Yet, six days later, Trump was back to his old lies: “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” he wrote on Truth Social. “How could the Polls be so wrong??? It’s all about the machines, which are far more important than the voter!”

This weekend Trump was at it again. He called Democrats’ recent electoral sweep a “rather strange ‘win.’”

items.title: Tell Congress to protect funding for those unhoused.
items.author: SRS0=zgbh=JL=mail135.sea51.mcsv.net=bounce-mc.us19_228507186.17295082-8782042e9f@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content:
Late Thursday night, the Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, by a vote of 62-33 (Native News Online). The bill would speed up federal permits for data centers, pipelines, wind and solar farms, and mines (Utah Public Radio). More than 70 Tribal Nations came out against it, because its third section would weaken the law that gives them agency when a project threatens their sacred places (NCAI). The legislation passed in the Senate on Thursday, and will be considered by the House when it returns from Thanksgiving recess (Native News Online).

The law at stake is Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, passed in 1966. It requires federal agencies to consider how their projects affect historic places, and to invite tribes into the process when those places carry religious and cultural meaning for them (ACHP). To be clear, it's a modest protection. The final decision still rests with the federal agency, not the tribe (ACHP). But it's often the only seat tribes get at the table, especially since many sacred sites sit outside reservation boundaries (Native News Online).

The bill would narrow which projects need that review in the first place, decrease touch points for tribal input, and make it harder for tribes to get a court to pause a project before the damage is done (NARF). "This is such an existential threat to Indian Country," National Congress of American Indians President Mark Macarro said at a press conference earlier this month (Native News Online). The bill was introduced in September with no public hearings and no tribal consultation (Native News Online).

The legislation also deems natural features like mountains, bodies of water and landscapes ineligible as historic property (Turtle Talk). For many tribes, those are the types of places that are sacred. Beyond that, it expands the scope of the federal government to misuse these natural resources, potentially covering even more resources from the communities that need them most.

Native people have fought for generations for the right to pray on their own land. Congress passed the American Indian Religious Freedom Act in 1978, after finding that federal and state laws often disrupted Native religious practices (The Conversation). But ten years later, the Supreme Court ruled that the Forest Service could build a road through the Chimney Rock area of Northern California, land sacred to the Yurok, Karuk and Tolowa peoples (Oyez). The Court called the harm to their religion "incidental" and treated the 1978 law as a policy without real legal protection (Oyez, The Conversation). In his dissent, Justice William Brennan wrote that "Native American faith is inextricably bound to the use of land" (The Conversation).

Oak Flat, or Chi'chil Biłdagoteel, in Arizona, is used for religious and coming-of-age ceremonies by The San Carlos Apache and other tribes. The land was protected from mining by a 1955 order from President Eisenhower (Cronkite News). In 2014, the late Sen. John McCain slipped a provision into a defense bill to trade 2,422 acres of it to Resolution Copper (Cronkite News). The Supreme Court declined to hear Apache Stronghold's appeal last year, and the Forest Service handed over the land on March 16 (Cronkite News). The mine would leave a crater more than 1,000 feet deep and up to two miles across (Cronkite). Legislation like BAAJA will make it even harder for tribes to be heard and respected in these decisions.

This week, many of us will sit down for a holiday that misconstrues how colonizers disrespected Native communities and their land. That practice — of expulsion and displacement, of extraction and suppression — is still happening today. Use this week to help write a new story, and support contemporary Native issues with the gratitude and reverence they deserve.

items.content:
We are a century-strong grassroots movement working to empower voters and defend democracy. Originally referred to as a “mighty political experiment,” the League has paved the way for women’s suffrage, launched an ongoing fight for equal rights — and changed our democracy forever.

We’re the League of Women Voters. And we’re so glad to have you with us.

We’re grateful for your involvement in our mission to ensure every voter has the tools and opportunity to make their voice heard. Your support ensures that every eligible voter has free and fair access to the ballot box, that voters pick our leaders instead of the other way around, and that the people hold our elected officials accountable.

The work of the League of Women Voters does not stop between elections. League members are on the ground 365 days a year, working to register, educate, mobilize, and protect voters so we can build a more inclusive, representative democracy.

Today, you’re embracing the League's mission at an especially critical time. Attacks on voting rights have been coming to us from all directions. And we are fighting back.

The League is defending democracy at every level of government: federal, state, and local. With Leagues in every Congressional jurisdiction, we have the widespread reach and people power to create change on a national level. And we're proud to be a source of trusted, nonpartisan election information for millions of voters. Together, we are protecting voters and building civic power in every corner of the country — including yours.

Thank you again for your commitment to empowering voters and defending our democracy — ensuring our electorate reflects the wonderfully diverse communities across our country. We’re glad you’re with us!

items.title: A hospital slashed costs. Then a patient froze to death on its roof.
items.author: bounce-mc.us1_388705.10709053-d186966748@mail194.suw241.rsgsv.net
items.content:
When a new healthcare company took over a struggling hospital in Waukegan, Illinois, residents hoped it would finally revitalize the facility. Vista Medical Center East had already been bought and sold four times—but maybe this time would be different. 

The new owner was American Healthcare Systems, a for-profit company pitching itself as a turnaround specialist for distressed hospitals. Rick Harris, a local pastor and businessman on the hospital’s board, had never heard of it. And his research turned up a troubling example of its work: A year before, AHS took over a struggling hospital in St. Louis. When financial troubles there got worse instead of better, AHS closed it in less than a year.

“I’m just thinking to myself, if I’ve got good intentions, if I can’t pay for this hospital, if I owe all of this money…then where am I getting the money to buy Vista?” he said.

Soon, AHS was stiffing vendors, not paying doctors, and leaving millions in taxes unpaid. It asked the state of Illinois for money and got $30 million in loans. AHS promised this money would allow it to pay staff and keep Vista running smoothly. 

But what happened instead would shine a spotlight on the hospital, AHS, and the for-profit playbook in American healthcare. A 28-year-old woman who came to the ER was found on the roof of the hospital in a gown and socks, frozen to death. 

, in an investigation produced in collaboration with the McGraw Center for Business Journalism at CUNY's Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism, we find out how her death happened and the financial chaos that laid the groundwork.

items.title: We built our own platform for this moment
items.author: 1axbtwoq239im3vds5bhycqyj7inh0vraysn9v@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Shortly after the election, I came to you with a bold prediction: once all the ballots were counted and the results certified, Democrats would hold 56 Senate seats. I can now report that my prediction came true.

Throughout the post-election period, I have worn two hats. I am the chairman of Elias Law Group, the law firm that helped secure the final victories. I am also the founder of Democracy Docket, an outlet that had reporters on the ground.

During that time, Democracy Docket provided you with in-depth reporting, analysis and commentary on what was happening and what to expect next. There was no hedging, no false equivalence and no both-sides journalism.

When Mississippi’s secretary of state tried to blame third-party vendors for high rates of ballots flagged for further review, rather than counted outright, Democracy Docket covered it. When the Department of Justice threatened, and then abandoned, a legal effort to block Alaska’s certification, Democracy Docket cut through the spin and told you what was really at stake.

Throughout it all, I offered my analysis in writing and on video podcasts. Thanks to support from its premium members, Democracy Docket dropped its paywall from Election Day until the Alaska race was called.

During that period, one of the most visited parts of the Democracy Docket website was its live blog, which kept you updated on the remaining races to be called. It featured a mix of short and long written pieces, along with video reports from the states.

Democracy Docket could provide this feature for free because it built its own technology platform. That may seem minor, but think about what it meant in practice.

If we had relied on a corporate platform that decided, under political pressure, to restrict or remove us, you could have lost access to that live blog in the middle of the Alaska fight, precisely when accurate information mattered most.

That is why Democracy Docket built its own custom technology stack: to ensure it is never beholden to venture capital firms, tech CEOs or corporations whose interests and alliances shift with the wind. Honestly, this makes operating Democracy Docket harder, more expensive and often a headache.

But managing our own platform is another way we ensure Democracy Docket stays fiercely independent and unapologetically pro-democracy. It makes it far harder for any one company to be pressured by Donald Trump into cutting us off, and far harder for any one vendor to cripple us.

There are other benefits as well.

It is never sold or traded, and you won’t receive emails urging you to sign up for some other site or product.

There are no Nazis on Democracy Docket, no right-wing propaganda and no one promoting crypto schemes.

, our subscribers and members, including by hosting a live blog in the middle of a critical election.

Across the country, we’ve watched media owners and executives curry favor with Trump, trading tough coverage for access or bowing to the fear of lawsuits, investigations and prosecution. Democracy Docket is built to withstand those pressures.

Democracy Docket is powered by premium members who pay $120 a year, just $10 a month, for access to all of its content. It simply cannot do its work without them. If you are able, please consider joining the more than 70,000 members who make this work possible.

We have fought long and hard for this victory, but this is not the end of the road. Donald Trump is still in the White House. The weaponization of government against Trump’s political opponents is escalating.

Democracy Docket will be there every step of the way. I am proud to have you on our team.

Persistence. The willingness to keep doing the work, generation after generation, as the challenges change and the stakes evolve.

Today, Americans United celebrates 79 years of doing exactly that. Over nearly eight decades, AU has helped end government-sponsored prayer and Bible reading in public schools, challenged religious discrimination, defended LGBTQ+ equality and reproductive freedom, and brought countless cases protecting the separation of church and state.

We also have some incredible news to share with you: In a win for religious freedom and church-state separation, a federal judge issued a preliminary injunction yesterday in our lawsuit, blocking U.S. Department of Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins from continuing to proselytize 100,000 USDA employees. 

This crucial decision sends a message to the Trump administration that it cannot misuse taxpayer resources to preach, hold government-sponsored prayer services during work time, and broadcast Christian Nationalism over official communication channels.

This important win – and celebrating another year of Americans United – is what persistence looks like to me. It’s not simply staying in the work, but building the people and institutions that will sustain it for generations to come.

Friend, help us carry this work forward.

items.title: Big Law sold out to save itself
items.author: 1axcjxcfssq191s8m1y2gqeprvibr72b7trmjn@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
When Donald Trump’s executive orders and Department of Justice lawsuits attacked voting and elections, Big Law was nowhere to be found. Yet when Trump needed free legal services, at least one law firm, Kirkland & Ellis, was there to help.

In April 2025, to avoid a punishing executive order, Kirkland agreed to provide $125 million in free legal work for causes the White House supported. It was one of nine Big Law firms that together pledged $940 million under similar deals.

Now we know what some of that work looked like.

According to news reports, Kirkland provided nearly $12 million in free legal services, totaling more than 6,400 hours, to agencies including the Commerce and Defense Departments. In addition, according to MSNOW, the firm “also estimated that it has done $18.7 million in free legal work for outside clients in the causes Trump listed in the Truth Social post announcing the deal.”

Importantly, Kirkland is only the first of the nine firms to provide this information to Democratic members of the House and Senate, who are preparing to conduct oversight on the issue. We have not yet heard from Paul Weiss, which led Big Law’s capitulation to Trump, or from the other firms that seemed eager to get in on the action.

Kirkland wants us to believe it was the victim of a threat.

items.title: How homelessness and racism intersect.
items.author: SRS0=kL4K=JH=mail70.suw17.mcsv.net=bounce-mc.us19_228507186.17295061-8782042e9f@eforward.registrar-servers.com
items.content:
Homelessness Funding Is on the Line. Here’s How to Protect It.

Today, the National Alliance to End Homelessness is leading a national day of action to protect federal homelessness funding (National Alliance to End Homelessness). Advocates are asking Congress to add a few lines to its next spending bill that would require the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to renew every Continuum of Care project expiring this fiscal year for 12 months, without a new competition (National Low Income Housing Coalition).

The Continuum of Care program is the largest federal source of money for local homelessness work. It pays for programs like permanent supportive housing, where people get a stable home along with services like health care and job support (National Low Income Housing Coalition), and transitional housing, which gives people a safe place to stay while they look for a permanent home (National Association of Counties).

The Trump administration has spent the past year trying to limit spending on homelessness. In July 2025, the president signed an executive order directing agencies to end support for Housing First policies, which give people a permanent home quickly without first requiring sobriety, treatment or a job (The White House). But Housing First has been federal policy under presidents of both parties since 2003 (Associated Press), and it has proven to be the most effective way to rehouse people (National Alliance to End Homelessness).

HUD then wrote new rules for this year’s Continuum of Care grants that put the president’s order into practice. In August, a federal judge ruled that those rules were unlawful. HUD had set aside $1.3 billion of this year’s funding for new transitional housing and service-only projects, a change that would have cut money from many programs already keeping people housed (National Association of Counties). The judge also struck down rules that required programs to follow the president’s executive orders and restricted diversity efforts. But in September, an appeals court let HUD move forward while it considers the case. Under HUD’s plan, only 60 percent of funding would be protected for renewals, down from nearly 90 percent. Advocates estimate that 97,000 people who were once unhoused could lose their housing as a result (National Low Income Housing Coalition).

The delays are already hurting people. In Los Angeles, providers that serve domestic violence survivors and unhoused people have cut staff and drained their reserves while HUD held up their grants (LAist). As of September, more than 1,300 renewal grant agreements across the country, about one in five, had not been fully executed. “If HUD doesn’t start to reimburse agencies quickly … we’re going to see more suffering on the street,” said Myong Kim of the Downtown Women’s Center in Los Angeles.

The people impacted by these funding cuts are disproportionately people of color. Black people are 14 percent of the U.S. population but 33 percent of people experiencing homelessness. Latino people make up 27.5 percent of the unhoused population, and Native and Pacific Islander people are also overrepresented. These numbers reflect generations of policy, from redlining to exclusionary zoning to landlords and lenders who still screen people out by eviction records and criminal background (National Alliance to End Homelessness). Today, Black renters are 28 percent of renters in the places Eviction Lab tracks, but 39 percent of the people facing eviction (Eviction Lab).

While funding for housing is under attack, more places are choosing punishment instead. Since the Supreme Court’s 2024 ruling in Grants Pass v. Johnson, more than 350 cities and 14 states have adopted tougher laws on street homelessness (Stateline). In 2022, we spoke with Jamaal of ACT UP Philadelphia about the violence of encampment sweeps (Anti-Racism Daily). “Philly says all the time, ‘We can’t afford to house people, the housing is too expensive,’ but every time we turn around, they increase funding to the police,” he told us. I think about that line a lot, because it’s still true in so many cities.

To be clear, renewing these grants won’t end homelessness on its own. We still need far more affordable homes, higher wages and an end to policies that punish people for being poor. But keeping existing programs running is the least Congress can do, and it’s within reach this month. If you have five minutes today, I encourage you to send that email. For many families, these few lines in a spending bill could decide whether they stay housed this winter.

items.title: Trump lost the race he bet everything on
items.author: 1axbqhwmo0qcdwqoqfjj3xipe99odyaoflv15f@bf56x.hubspotemail.net
items.content:
Last night, Mary Peltola officially won Alaska’s Senate race. The Division of Elections updated its results to show she held an outright majority. The outcome is undeniable.

With Peltola’s victory, Donald Trump lost the one fight he cared about most.

For months, Trump obsessed over this race. Even as he watched Republicans get swept from coast to coast, his focus stayed fixed on Alaska.

Weighed down by his historic unpopularity, his party lost Senate seats in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina, Ohio and South Carolina. Even Mississippi.

State after state, as the election returns came in, Trump could do nothing to stop the bleeding.

Yet, as his party imploded, Trump seethed and raged about Sen. Dan Sullivan’s looming defeat in Alaska.

He spread misinformation about how Alaskans vote. He lied about the results, insisting that votes cast for a different candidate belonged to the incumbent.

He ordered his Justice Department to sue to block certification. When my law firm beat back that lawsuit, the DOJ came after me personally. Trump went on national television and said I should go to jail.

None of these attacks changed the vote count. With each new batch of ballots, Peltola’s lead grew.

Last night, the dam broke.

Peltola now leads by 12,458 votes. More importantly, she has won more than half of all the votes cast in the race.

There will be no ranked-choice tabulation, and no room for conspiracy theories about whose votes “really” belonged to whom.

And with that, Trump’s lies collapse once and for all.

Sullivan’s campaign says he won’t concede until the results are certified. The campaign insists it will “let that process run its course until every legal vote is counted and certified.”

Fortunately, election results are stubborn. The numbers are what they are. They do not require a concession to be accurate. They do not care about the losing candidate’s feelings or his stage of grief.

Despite all of Trump’s bluster, Mary Peltola will be the next senator from Alaska. A Yup’ik Alaskan and former congresswoman, she made history in 2022 as the first Alaska Native elected to Congress. She will be sworn in on Jan. 3, 2027, with the rest of the newly elected class.

She will join a radically changed Congress. In the House, Democrats will hold a historic 260-seat majority. But it is the 56 seats in the Senate that have truly upended Trump’s agenda.

With margins like these, Trump will no longer be able to confirm his cronies and sycophants. His judicial nominees will languish. Any Supreme Court vacancy will remain unfilled.

With 56 seats, Democrats won’t just control the Senate for the next two years. They are almost certain to hold the majority for the next four. And if a Democrat wins the presidency in 2028, a Democratic Senate will be ready to fill every vacancy Trump leaves behind.

Trump will fare no better with his legislative agenda. Democrats in Congress will decide which bills reach his desk. Trump will be reduced to nothing more than a signature — signing or vetoing the bills placed before him.

The question remains: Why Alaska? Of all the defeats and humiliations Trump suffered this year, why did Dan Sullivan’s loss sting the most?

Trump will say it’s because he believes Democrats cheated. But Trump has never cared about cheating.

In 2020, he told Georgia’s secretary of state to “find” 11,780 votes that did not exist. In September, he stood before the Republican convention in Dallas and instructed his supporters to “cheat like hell” in this year’s elections. 

In any event, Trump’s lies are no longer sustainable. We now know that Peltola won an outright majority. No theory about confused voters or a second Dan Sullivan can explain away a candidate who won more votes than everyone else combined.

The simplest answer is the most likely. Trump’s focus on Alaska is the fixation of an elderly man whose mental faculties are declining.

It is the same fixation that has caused him to dedicate his presidency to a White House ballroom, a public golf course in Washington, D.C., and a triumphal arch. All while his party burned.

Whatever the reason, Trump bet everything on Alaska, and he lost. For the rest of us, Peltola’s victory is cause for celebration. Let’s take a moment to enjoy it.
